newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission faces BSE censure motion.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission faces BSE censure motion.

text.p: Belgian Socialist Jose Happart presented a motion to the European Parliament on Thursday censuring the European Commission for seriously mismanaging the European Union's mad cow crisis.

Parliamentary sources said Happart had found the 63 signatures needed to force a vote of censure which would be taken within 48 hours of parliament debating its highly critical report of the EU executive.
The debate on the report into the management of the crisis caused by the spread of the disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), is currently set for Wednesday.
The sources said it was unlikely that Happart, the most radical member of the special commitee of inquiry which drew up the report, would win mainstream support.
A censure motion needs the backing of two-thirds of votes cast in the 626-member assembly in order to force the resignation of Commission President Jacques Santer and his 19 colleagues.

Last week the 19-member cross party committee resoundingly rejected a more moderate move by the Green Group under which a censure vote would have been taken only if the Commission failed to take corrective measures by December 1997.
In a letter to Parliament President Jose Maria Gil Robles, Happart said the Commission should be sanctioned for failing to give public health priority over economic needs.
It atacked the incoherence of "pseudo-political decisions" and what it described as "pseudo-scientific" advice.
It also criticised the Commission for being deliberately passive towards Britain, adding that it gave way to "political and industrial pressure from the beef sector."
The Commission was also attacked for failing to cooperate with the committee of inquiry.
In an unsuccessful bid to prevent the threat of censure from the parliament, Santer on Wednesday pushed through a major reorganisation of the Commission's food safety services.

The high-profile consumer affairs commissioner, Emma Bonino, was given responsibility for ensuring that public health will be properly protected as well as control of a new veterinary inspection office based in Ireland.

But the parliament is pressing for more radical action, including possible legal action against Britain which it holds mainly responsible for the crisis which erupted last March after London said BSE could be transmitted to humans.

Unless Santer comes up with a pledge of tougher political measures next week, a second censure motion, which has already gathered more than 100 signatures, could be tabled, parliamentary sources said.
